Image Processing · Lab 04 · Material

Geometric Transformations

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Move and rotate the desk drawing while keeping its landmarks attached to the right locations. Treat the transform, destination canvas and border policy as one reproducible geometric record.

What you will learn

  • Apply translations, rotations and three-point affine transforms.
  • Distinguish a source-to-destination map from destination-to-source sampling.
  • Compose transforms before resampling and calculate an expanded canvas.
  • Transform keypoints with the image and record their visibility explicitly.

Before this lab: Complete Lab 03 and understand array dimensions, interpolation and coordinate conventions.

In this lab

  1. Translation matrices
  2. Rotation about a chosen center
  3. Expanded rotation canvases
  4. Border policies and observed content
  5. Affine maps from three control points
  6. Forward maps and inverse sampling
  7. Composition and single resampling
  8. Keypoint visibility and provenance

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Run once. Geometry below uses pixel-center coordinates: x increases right, y increases down, and (0,0) is the first pixel center.

Python · shared setup
import io
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
import numpy as np
import cv2
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageOps, UnidentifiedImageError
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cv2.setNumThreads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(204)

# Original 192-by-128 desk drawing with text, fine lines and a textured background.
h, w = 128, 192
yy, xx = np.mgrid[:h, :w]
wood = 180 + 18*xx/(w-1) + 6*np.sin(yy*0.7) + 3*np.sin(xx*0.23)
background = np.stack([wood+20, wood, wood-28], axis=-1)
scene = Image.fromarray(np.clip(background,0,255).astype(np.uint8))
draw = ImageDraw.Draw(scene)
draw.rectangle((12,20,80,108), fill=(166,45,52), outline=(72,25,31), width=2)
draw.rectangle((14,22,23,106), fill=(105,32,44))
draw.rectangle((26,32,72,56), fill=(239,228,198))
draw.text((31,39),"NOTES", fill=(35,42,52))
for y in range(92,107,3):
    draw.line((26,y,77,y),fill=(231,219,190),width=1)
draw.rectangle((88,7,127,43),fill=(241,216,82),outline=(148,115,29))
draw.text((94,13),"TO DO",fill=(45,44,31))
for y in [27,32,37]:
    draw.line((94,y,120,y),fill=(100,94,56))
draw.ellipse((162,60,188,98),outline=(235,237,224),width=7)

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

Translation matrices

A translation moves every location by the same horizontal and vertical offsets. With image coordinates increasing right and down, adding 18 to x moves a point right, while subtracting 9 from y moves it upward. A two-by-three affine matrix writes both operations together: its first two columns act on x and y, and its final column supplies the offsets.

Pass this source-to-destination matrix to warpAffine without the inverse-map flag. OpenCV handles destination sampling internally. The destination size remains the original width and height, so some source content leaves the canvas and new locations require a border value. Use nearest interpolation here because an integer translation can copy retained pixel values exactly; this isolates geometry from blended sampling. Mark a known book point before and after translation using the same matrix. Moving the image without moving the point would produce a geometrically inconsistent record even if each array had a valid shape. Keep the original image so that clipped content remains available outside this particular output.

Try it

  1. Build a translation of +18 horizontally and -9 vertically.
  2. Warp onto the original-size canvas with explicit padding.
  3. Transform and overlay the same book keypoint.
Python · run in order
translation = np.array([[1,0,18],[0,1,-9]],dtype=np.float64)
shifted = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,translation,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
point = np.array([40.0,44.0])
shifted_point = translation@np.append(point,1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.5))
for ax,image,p,title in zip(axes,[rgb,shifted],[point,shifted_point],["Source","Right 18, up 9"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.scatter([p[0]],[p[1]],marker="+",s=90,c="cyan")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The marker stays attached to the book because it follows the image geometry. The left and bottom padding are newly supplied pixels, and some top/right source content has left this fixed canvas.

Change and compare

  • Change the vertical offset to positive and predict the movement direction.
  • Check a retained pixel pair numerically before judging the whole image.

Guided task 02

Rotation about a chosen center

A rotation needs a center, an angle and a destination canvas. For integer-centered image coordinates, the midpoint of a width-by-height grid is ((width-1)/2,(height-1)/2). This differs by half a pixel from the midpoint of an outer-edge coordinate range. Keeping the convention explicit prevents small systematic shifts.

OpenCV's getRotationMatrix2D uses angles in degrees, with positive angles rotating counterclockwise in the displayed image. Rotate the desk by 25 degrees around its grid midpoint and retain the original canvas. Linear interpolation supplies values at fractional source positions. Transform the mug point with the returned matrix and plot it on the rotated image. The center remains fixed by construction, but the canvas does not automatically grow to contain every rotated corner. That distinction separates the mathematical map from the representation we choose to store. An apparently missing corner may therefore be an expected consequence of the canvas rather than a wrong angle. Inspect the border and retain the matrix when later coordinates must be mapped back.

Try it

  1. Calculate the center in pixel-center coordinates.
  2. Create a 25-degree rotation with unit scale.
  3. Map a mug keypoint and inspect fixed-canvas clipping.
Python · run in order
center = ((w-1)/2,(h-1)/2)
rotation = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center,25,1.0)
rotated = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,rotation,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
point = np.array([143.0,82.0])
rotated_point = rotation@np.append(point,1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.5))
for ax,image,p,title in zip(axes,[rgb,rotated],[point,rotated_point],["Source","25 degrees, fixed canvas"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.scatter([p[0]],[p[1]],marker="+",s=80,c="cyan")
    ax.scatter([center[0]],[center[1]],marker="x",s=45,c="yellow")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The yellow center stays fixed and the cyan point follows the mug. The fixed canvas cuts off some rotated source area while other output areas receive the stated padding colour.

Change and compare

  • Try -25 degrees and compare the rotation direction.
  • Rotate around the book point instead, then verify that this chosen point remains fixed.

Guided task 03

Expanded rotation canvases

To keep the full rotated footprint, calculate where the source's outer corners land before allocating the destination. Our point coordinates refer to pixel centers, so the source's outer boundary lies half a pixel before the first center and half a pixel after the last. Its corners are therefore (-0.5,-0.5), (width-0.5,-0.5), and the corresponding bottom corners.

Transform all four corners, find their minimum and maximum coordinates and round the required span upward to integer dimensions. Then add an offset that puts the transformed minimum at the destination's outer edge -0.5. This is a canvas adjustment composed with the original rotation, not a second rotation. The final image is resampled once using the adjusted matrix. The rounded canvas may have a small additional margin on the far sides. It now contains the source footprint, while still needing padding in regions outside the rotated source. This method makes the coordinate reasoning visible and avoids guessing a large enough square. It also illustrates why transforming only two opposite corners is insufficient once an axis-aligned rectangle is rotated.

Try it

  1. Rotate all four outer corners by 32 degrees.
  2. Compute integer canvas dimensions from their full span.
  3. Shift the matrix to the expanded canvas and warp once.
Python · run in order
base_rotation = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(((w-1)/2,(h-1)/2),32,1.0)
outer_corners = np.array([[-0.5,-0.5],[w-0.5,-0.5],[w-0.5,h-0.5],[-0.5,h-0.5]])
homogeneous = np.column_stack([outer_corners,np.ones(4)])
rotated_corners = homogeneous@base_rotation.T
minimum = rotated_corners.min(axis=0)
maximum = rotated_corners.max(axis=0)
out_w,out_h = np.ceil(maximum-minimum).astype(int)
expanded_matrix = base_rotation.copy()
expanded_matrix[:,2] += -0.5-minimum
expanded = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,expanded_matrix,(int(out_w),int(out_h)),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
mapped_corners = homogeneous@expanded_matrix.T
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,4.3))
axes[0].imshow(rgb)
axes[0].set_title("Source footprint")
axes[1].imshow(expanded)
closed = np.vstack([mapped_corners,mapped_corners[:1]])
axes[1].plot(closed[:,0],closed[:,1],color="cyan",linewidth=1)
axes[1].set_title("Expanded canvas, one warp")
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The cyan polygon follows the rotated source boundary inside the expanded output. Padding surrounds it, but source corners are no longer lost solely because the destination stayed at its old size.

Change and compare

  • Compare the expanded dimensions for positive and negative versions of the same angle.
  • Transform only two opposite corners as a calculation exercise and explain why their bounds can be incomplete.

Guided task 04

Border policies and observed content

A warp asks for source samples corresponding to destination locations. Some requested locations lie outside the source. A constant border supplies a fixed colour; replication extends the nearest edge value; reflection mirrors nearby source content. Each is an explicit extrapolation rule, not a newly observed part of the desk.

Translate the drawing 20 pixels right and 14 down with nearest interpolation to isolate those rules. Compare constant, replicated and reflected borders. A separate coverage mask is created by warping an all-one source with constant-zero padding. Its zero region identifies destination locations that did not come from the original source footprint in this integer example. Replicated or reflected colours may look continuous, but their visual plausibility does not change that coverage. This distinction matters when padding could be mistaken for another object or measured area. Record the border mode with the transform rather than accepting a library default silently. For fractional interpolation, a binary coverage map alone would not describe the full mixture of valid and border samples; this activity deliberately uses an integer shift to keep that interpretation exact.

Try it

  1. Apply the same integer translation with three border modes.
  2. Warp an all-one source mask using constant-zero padding.
  3. Compare extrapolated appearances with actual source coverage.
Python · run in order
shift = np.array([[1,0,20],[0,1,14]],dtype=np.float64)
constant = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,shift,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
replicated = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,shift,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REPLICATE)
reflected = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,shift,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
coverage = cv2.warpAffine(np.ones((h,w),dtype=np.uint8),shift,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,4,figsize=(12,3.3))
for ax,image,title in zip(axes[:3],[constant,replicated,reflected],["Constant padding","Replicated edge","Reflected edge"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
axes[3].imshow(coverage,cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=1)
axes[3].set_title("Copied source coverage")
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The first three panels invent different border appearances outside the same valid region. The coverage panel prevents those appearances from being confused with newly captured scene content.

Change and compare

  • Compare BORDER_REFLECT with BORDER_REFLECT_101 near the first row.
  • Inspect how a repeated label near an edge could be misleading under reflection.

Guided task 05

Affine maps from three control points

An affine transform can combine translation, rotation, scaling and shear. Three non-collinear source points and their three corresponding destination points determine such a map in two dimensions. Collinear points do not constrain the full plane, so choose a triangle with nonzero area. The point order expresses correspondence: the first source point must match the first destination point.

Use three corners of the notebook's pale label and move them to a deliberately skewed triangle. OpenCV's getAffineTransform expects matching float32 point arrays. Apply the resulting map to the entire desk, rather than separately moving or painting the label. Straight lines remain straight under an affine map, and parallel source lines remain parallel, but lengths and angles need not be preserved. This is a controlled desk-view deformation, not a general correction for every perspective photograph; a general projective mapping needs a different model. Plot the numbered control points before and after the warp and verify their numeric correspondence. A plausible-looking image cannot detect a mistaken correspondence as reliably as checking those known points.

Try it

  1. Define ordered source and destination triangles.
  2. Estimate their affine map and warp the whole drawing.
  3. Overlay the corresponding points and verify their transformed positions.
Python · run in order
source_points = np.array([[26,32],[72,32],[26,56]],dtype=np.float32)
destination_points = np.array([[30,28],[86,35],[24,60]],dtype=np.float32)
affine = cv2.getAffineTransform(source_points,destination_points)
warped = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,affine,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
mapped_points = np.column_stack([source_points,np.ones(3)])@affine.T
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.7))
for ax,image,points,title in zip(axes,[rgb,warped],[source_points,mapped_points],["Source control triangle","Destination control triangle"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    closed = np.vstack([points,points[:1]])
    ax.plot(closed[:,0],closed[:,1],"c+-",linewidth=1)
    for index,p in enumerate(points):
        ax.text(p[0]+3,p[1]-3,str(index+1),color="cyan",fontsize=10)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Each numbered source point lands on its paired destination. The surrounding desk changes under the same global affine map, so this operation also changes other objects and the source footprint.

Change and compare

  • Swap two destination correspondences and inspect the resulting geometry.
  • Use a destination triangle with doubled horizontal distances and describe the effect on the surrounding scene.

Guided task 06

Forward maps and inverse sampling

A forward map answers where a source point lands. Image resampling usually asks the opposite question: for each output pixel, which source position should supply its value? These are related by an inverse transform. Confusing the two directions can produce a coherent-looking warp in the wrong direction, rather than a clear error message.

Use an invertible shear-and-translation matrix. The ordinary warpAffine call takes this forward matrix and obtains the inverse sampling map internally. Alternatively, pass the explicitly inverted matrix together with WARP_INVERSE_MAP. These two routes describe the same geometry. Passing the forward matrix while also setting that flag is the deliberate failure example in the third panel. Map a known point forward and then backward to verify the coordinate contract separately from the images. The inverse restores point coordinates for an invertible affine map, but warping an already resampled image backward is not guaranteed to restore its original pixels. Interpolation, clipping and borders can have discarded information even when the matrix itself has a perfectly valid inverse.

Try it

  1. Construct one invertible forward affine matrix.
  2. Compare normal forward use with explicit inverse-map use.
  3. Check a point round trip and inspect the wrongly flagged call.
Python · run in order
forward = np.array([[1,0.25,12],[0,1,-6]],dtype=np.float64)
inverse = cv2.invertAffineTransform(forward)
ordinary = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,forward,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
explicit_inverse = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,inverse,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR|cv2.WARP_INVERSE_MAP,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
wrong_direction = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,forward,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR|cv2.WARP_INVERSE_MAP,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
source_point = np.array([40.0,44.0])
destination_point = forward@np.append(source_point,1)
recovered_point = inverse@np.append(destination_point,1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(11,3.4))
for ax,image,title in zip(axes,[ordinary,explicit_inverse,wrong_direction],["Forward matrix, normal flag","Inverse matrix, inverse flag","Forward plus inverse flag: wrong"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title,fontsize=10)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The first two panels represent the same sampling route. The third interprets the supplied coefficients in the opposite direction, so valid numbers alone do not establish the intended geometry.

Change and compare

  • Verify another point using forward then inverse multiplication.
  • Explain why a point round trip can be exact while an image round trip loses detail.

Guided task 07

Composition and single resampling

Several geometric decisions can be combined before creating a new pixel array. In homogeneous coordinates, extend each two-by-three affine matrix with a final row [0,0,1]. If transform A happens first and B second, the combined forward matrix is B multiplied by A for column-vector points. Reversing the order generally describes a different operation.

Two half-pixel translations make a particularly clear sampling comparison. Applying each one separately with linear interpolation blends the image twice. Composing their matrices first yields a one-pixel translation that can be sampled once. The final coordinate displacement is the same, but the pixel arrays need not match because interpolation is not an exact reversible operation. Compare the source, the sequential result, the single-warp result and their absolute difference. The one-pixel route in this controlled case preserves retained source samples exactly. This demonstrates the cost of unnecessary resampling, not a guarantee that every one-pass transform produces a sharper or more useful result. Retain transform metadata and the original array so that a chain of edits can be rendered from the source when possible.

Try it

  1. Create two translations of half a pixel on both axes.
  2. Compare sequential linear warps with a composed one-pixel warp.
  3. Measure their difference after safe promotion.
Python · run in order
first = np.array([[1,0,0.5],[0,1,0.5],[0,0,1]],dtype=np.float64)
second = np.array([[1,0,0.5],[0,1,0.5],[0,0,1]],dtype=np.float64)
combined = second@first
intermediate = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,first[:2],(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
sequential = cv2.warpAffine(intermediate,second[:2],(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
single = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,combined[:2],(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
difference = np.max(np.abs(sequential.astype(np.int16)-single.astype(np.int16)),axis=2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,4,figsize=(12,3.3))
for ax,image,title in zip(axes[:3],[rgb,sequential,single],["Source","Two fractional warps","One composed warp"]):
    ax.imshow(image,interpolation="nearest")
    ax.set_title(title)
im = axes[3].imshow(difference,cmap="magma",vmin=0,vmax=max(1,int(difference.max())))
axes[3].set_title("Largest channel difference")
fig.colorbar(im,ax=axes[3],shrink=0.65)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The difference map shows that equal final coordinates do not imply equal resampled pixels. Fine strokes make repeated interpolation especially easy to inspect in this deliberately simple example.

Change and compare

  • Compose a rotation followed by translation and compare it with the reversed order.
  • Inspect only the retained interior to separate interpolation differences from border effects.

Guided task 08

Keypoint visibility and provenance

A geometrically transformed point can leave the chosen output even when its arithmetic is correct. Clamping that point to the nearest border would move its meaning to a different location. Instead retain the transformed coordinate and store a separate visibility flag. Keeping the original row order also preserves its link to the named object.

Translate the scene left by 65 and down by 12. Transform three named source points with the same matrix and determine visibility using an explicit rule: a continuous pixel-center coordinate is considered visible here when x lies from 0 through width minus 1 and y from 0 through height minus 1, inclusive. This conservative center-range rule is stated rather than mixed with an outer-edge box convention. Plot only visible points on the output, but keep all coordinates in the numeric record. The book point leaves the frame while the other two remain. Visibility is not evidence that an object is fully retained: a point may remain inside even if part of the associated object is cropped away. Preserve the distinction between a point test and a whole-object retention policy.

Try it

  1. Transform three named pixel-center landmarks.
  2. Compute an explicit visibility mask without clamping coordinates.
  3. Overlay visible landmarks while retaining every numeric row.
Python · run in order
names = ["book","mug","desk corner"]
points = np.array([[40,44],[143,82],[180,15]],dtype=np.float64)
matrix_shift = np.array([[1,0,-65],[0,1,12]],dtype=np.float64)
moved = cv2.warpAffine(rgb,matrix_shift,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST,borderMode=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT,borderValue=(35,45,55))
mapped = np.column_stack([points,np.ones(len(points))])@matrix_shift.T
def visible_centers(coordinates,width,height):
    return (coordinates[:,0]>=0)&(coordinates[:,0]<=width-1)&(coordinates[:,1]>=0)&(coordinates[:,1]<=height-1)
visible = visible_centers(mapped,w,h)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.7))
for ax,image,coordinates,keep,title in zip(axes,[rgb,moved],[points,mapped],[np.ones(3,dtype=bool),visible],["Named source points","Visible output points"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    for index in np.flatnonzero(keep):
        p = coordinates[index]
        ax.scatter([p[0]],[p[1]],c="cyan",marker="+",s=70)
        ax.text(p[0]+2,p[1]-4,names[index],color="cyan",fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.5,w-0.5)
    ax.set_ylim(h-0.5,-0.5)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
print("Mapped points:",mapped,"Visibility:",visible)

Read the result

An invisible point remains in the record with its actual outside coordinate. The visibility mask controls display without silently changing the landmark's geometric meaning.

Change and compare

  • Translate a point exactly onto the last pixel center and check the inclusive boundary.
  • Compare point visibility with whether the entire mug remains inside the output.
